ngc-4889.desc: NGC 4889 is a giant elliptical galaxy, the largest and brightest in the central region of the Coma Cluster, about 300 million light-years away. Its major axis of 2.9 arcminutes corresponds to about 250,000 light-years. At its centre it hosts a black hole of 21 billion solar masses, among the most massive ever measured.

galassia-girino.name: Tadpole Galaxy
galassia-girino.desc: The Tadpole Galaxy (UGC 10214) is a distorted spiral about 420 million light-years away, in the constellation Draco. An encounter with a small compact galaxy tore from it a tail of stars and gas more than 280,000 light-years long. In the tail shine clusters of young blue stars, each with up to about a million stars.

strada-percorsa-dalla-terra-attorno-al-s.name: Distance travelled by the Earth around the Sun
strada-percorsa-dalla-terra-attorno-al-s.desc: Each year the Earth travels around the Sun along an orbit about 940 million km long, at a mean speed of 29.78 km/s. Multiplying by the 4.54 billion years of the planet's age gives about 4.3 billion billion km, equal to about 450,000 light-years. It is an estimate that assumes an orbit that has always been the same as today's.

distanza-di-andromeda.name: Distance of Andromeda
distanza-di-andromeda.desc: The Andromeda galaxy, or M31, is about 2.5 million light-years away and is the large galaxy nearest to the Milky Way. The light we see from it today therefore set off 2.5 million years ago. Despite the distance, the Hubble Space Telescope can pick out the individual stars of its disc.

ic-1101.name: IC 1101
ic-1101.desc: IC 1101 is the giant elliptical galaxy at the centre of the cluster Abell 2029, more than a billion light-years away. Very deep images from the Isaac Newton Telescope, described in a 2026 study not yet peer-reviewed, place the edge at 260 kiloparsecs from the centre, for a diameter of about 520 kiloparsecs, that is, 1.7 million light-years. Earlier estimates reached 5.6 million light-years, and the result depends on how the edge of the galaxy is defined.

ammasso-della-fornace.name: Fornax Cluster
ammasso-della-fornace.desc: The Fornax Cluster is a cluster of galaxies in the southern constellation of the same name, whose centre is about 65 million light-years from Earth. Its virial radius is about 0.7 megaparsecs, so the diameter is about 1.4 megaparsecs, that is, between 4.5 and 5 million light-years. It contains almost sixty large galaxies and a similar number of dwarf galaxies, with the giant galaxy NGC 1399 at its centre.

abell-2029.name: Abell 2029
abell-2029.desc: Abell 2029 is a very massive galaxy cluster about 1 billion light-years from Earth, with redshift 0.0767. X-ray observations by the Suzaku satellite measured its r200 radius, used as an estimate of the virial radius, at 1.92 megaparsecs: the diameter is therefore about 3.8 megaparsecs, equal to about 12.5 million light-years. It includes thousands of galaxies immersed in a gigantic cloud of hot gas.

gruppo-locale.name: Local Group
gruppo-locale.desc: The Local Group is the group of galaxies to which the Milky Way belongs and extends for almost 10 million light-years. The most massive members are Andromeda (M31) and the Milky Way, followed by the Triangulum Galaxy (M33). A 2012 census lists more than 100 galaxies within 3 megaparsecs of the Sun, almost all dwarfs, within and around the group.

ammasso-della-vergine.name: Virgo Cluster
ammasso-della-vergine.desc: The Virgo Cluster is the nearest large galaxy cluster, at 16.5 megaparsecs, that is, about 54 million light-years. Its virial radius is 6 degrees on the sky, equal to 1.72 megaparsecs: the diameter is therefore about 3.4 megaparsecs, that is, about 11 million light-years, although the cluster has no sharp edge. The classic catalogue of the cluster lists 2,096 galaxies.

alcioneo.name: Alcyoneus
alcioneo.desc: Alcyoneus is a giant radio galaxy discovered in images from the LOFAR radio telescope and described in 2022. Its radio lobes extend in projection for 4.99 megaparsecs, about 16 million light-years, and the true length is at least 5 megaparsecs. When discovered it was the largest known structure of galactic origin, a record that passed in 2024 to Porphyrion.

porphyrion.name: Porphyrion
porphyrion.desc: Porphyrion is a pair of plasma jets launched by a supermassive black hole in a galaxy 7.5 billion light-years away. Announced in 2024 with data from LOFAR, uGMRT and Keck, it extends for about 7 megaparsecs, that is, 23 million light-years, as much as 140 Milky Ways in a row. It is the largest structure produced by a galaxy observed so far.

yottametro.name: Yottametre
yottametro.desc: The yottametre (Ym) is 10^24 metres: the SI prefix yotta stands for a factor of 10^24. It corresponds to about 105.7 million light-years, that is, about 32.4 million parsecs. A gigaparsec equals almost 31 yottametres.

superammasso-della-vergine.name: Virgo Supercluster
superammasso-della-vergine.desc: The Virgo Supercluster, or Local Supercluster, is the flattened assembly of about 50 groups of galaxies, including the Local Group, centred on the Virgo Cluster. It has no sharp boundaries and its diameter is roughly estimated at about 100 million light-years, with a mass of about 10¹⁵ solar masses. In 2014 Laniakea was defined, a much more extended supercluster that also includes the Virgo Cluster.

distanza-del-grande-attrattore.name: Distance of the Great Attractor
distanza-del-grande-attrattore.desc: The Great Attractor is a region of space with an enormous concentration of mass, whose gravity dominates our part of the Universe. It is associated with the Norma galaxy cluster, which is about 220 million light-years away. The distance is approximate, because the zone lies behind the plane of the Milky Way, where stars and dust hide most of the objects.

vuoto-del-boote.name: Boötes Void
vuoto-del-boote.desc: The Boötes Void is a nearly spherical region almost devoid of galaxies in the direction of the constellation Boötes. The 1987 study that confirmed its existence gives it a radius of 62 megaparsecs, calculated however with a Hubble constant of 50 km/s per megaparsec. With today's values of the constant the diameter falls from about 400 to about 280 or 300 million light-years, so the figure of 330 million is only indicative.

scala-acustica-barionica.name: Baryon acoustic scale
scala-acustica-barionica.desc: Pressure waves in the early Universe left an imprint on the distribution of galaxies: pairs of galaxies tend to lie at a distance that today is about 500 million light-years. This known length serves as a standard ruler for measuring cosmic expansion. The 2025 DESI measurements, combined with other data, prefer a dark energy that changes over time, but with a significance between 2.8 and 4.2 sigma that is not enough to confirm it.

laniakea.name: Laniakea
laniakea.desc: Laniakea is the supercluster to which the Milky Way belongs, defined in 2014 by Brent Tully and colleagues as the volume within which the motions of galaxies converge inwards. It has a diameter of 160 megaparsecs, about 520 million light-years, and contains a mass of 10¹⁷ solar masses in about 100,000 large galaxies. The name comes from Hawaiian and combines the words for heaven and spacious.

distanza-del-superammasso-di-shapley.name: Distance of the Shapley Supercluster
distanza-del-superammasso-di-shapley.desc: The Shapley Supercluster, named after the astronomer Harlow Shapley, is about 650 million light-years away. It is one of the most massive concentrations of galaxies in the local Universe. The hot gas of its clusters emits X-rays, observed among others by the eROSITA telescope.

complesso-pesci-balena.name: Pisces–Cetus Complex
complesso-pesci-balena.desc: The Pisces–Cetus Supercluster Complex is a structure proposed by Brent Tully in 1986 and 1987, in which galaxy-rich clusters group into complexes of about 50 clusters. Tully estimates its extent at about 300 megaparsecs, that is, about 1 billion light-years, a value that depends on the Hubble constant adopted. According to the author our own region of the universe is also part of it, with the clusters concentrated on the plane traced by the nearby galaxies.

quipu.name: Quipu
quipu.desc: Quipu is a superstructure of galaxy clusters identified with a map of clusters observed in X-rays at distances between 130 and 250 megaparsecs and presented in 2025 by Hans Böhringer and colleagues. It is more than 400 megaparsecs long, that is, over 1.3 billion light-years, with an estimated mass of about 2 × 10¹⁷ solar masses. The authors describe it as the largest cosmic structure discovered so far.

grande-muraglia-sloan.name: Sloan Great Wall
grande-muraglia-sloan.desc: The Sloan Great Wall is a filament of galaxies identified in Sloan Digital Sky Survey data, at a median distance of about 310 megaparsecs, that is, about a billion light-years. Its observed length is 1.37 billion light-years, which becomes 450 megaparsecs in comoving coordinates. The authors of the measurement described it as the largest structure observed up to that time, 80% longer than the Great Wall discovered by Geller and Huchra.

supervuoto-di-eridano.name: Eridanus Supervoid
supervuoto-di-eridano.desc: The Eridanus Supervoid is a vast region poor in galaxies, about 3 billion light-years away, aligned with the Cold Spot of the cosmic microwave background. Those who identified it in 2015 give it a diameter of about 1.8 billion light-years, but the measured radius has an error of about 23%, so the diameter can range from about 1.6 to 2.5 billion light-years. According to later analyses, in the standard cosmological model the void explains only 10–20% of the observed cooling.

vuoto-kbc.name: KBC Void
vuoto-kbc.desc: The KBC void, named after Keenan, Barger and Cowie who proposed it in 2013, is a possible low-density region surrounding the Local Group out to about 300 megaparsecs. The diameter is therefore about 600 megaparsecs, that is, about 2 billion light-years, with a matter density estimated to be lower than average by about 46%. Its existence and depth are debated, also because such a void could affect the local measurement of the Hubble constant.

gigaparsec.name: Gigaparsec
gigaparsec.desc: The gigaparsec (Gpc) is a billion parsecs, that is, about 3.0857 × 10^25 metres. It corresponds to about 3.26 billion light-years. It is the unit used for the largest cosmological distances.

arco-gigante.name: Giant Arc
arco-gigante.desc: The Giant Arc is a nearly symmetrical arc-shaped structure in the constellation Boötes, over 9.2 billion light-years away, announced in 2021. It extends for about 1 gigaparsec, that is, about 3.3 billion light-years, and was found thanks to the absorption of magnesium in the spectra of more distant quasars. The authors estimate a statistical significance between 3 and 4.8 sigma depending on the method used and cautiously speak of a possible challenge to the cosmological principle.

huge-lqg.name: Huge-LQG
huge-lqg.desc: The Huge-LQG is a large group of 73 quasars at mean redshift 1.27, identified in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey catalogue and described in 2012. Its greatest dimension is about 1,240 megaparsecs, that is, about 4 billion light-years, while the characteristic size is about 500 megaparsecs. Its physical reality is disputed: a later analysis shows that the same algorithm finds even larger groupings in random distributions of points.

grande-muraglia-ercole-corona-boreale.name: Hercules–Corona Borealis Great Wall
grande-muraglia-ercole-corona-boreale.desc: The Hercules–Corona Borealis Great Wall is a concentration of gamma-ray bursts at redshift about 2, at a distance of about 10 billion light-years: 14 of the 31 bursts in that band fall in about an eighth of the sky. The authors estimate its extent between 2,000 and 3,000 megaparsecs, that is, between about 6.5 and 9.8 billion light-years. If real it would be the largest known structure, but the discoverers themselves write that new data are needed to establish whether it truly exists.

distanza-dell-hubble-deep-field.name: Distance of the Hubble Deep Field
distanza-dell-hubble-deep-field.desc: The Hubble Deep Field is a 1995 image of a tiny patch of sky, in which the Hubble Space Telescope revealed at least 1,500 galaxies, many about four billion times fainter than what the human eye sees. Some are seen as they were more than 10 billion years ago, perhaps less than a billion years after the Big Bang. The distance given, about 12.7 billion light-years, is therefore the light-travel path of the most remote ones and is an estimate, not a single measurement.

raggio-di-hubble.name: Hubble radius
raggio-di-hubble.desc: The Hubble radius is the distance at which, according to Hubble's law, space recedes from us at the speed of light: it is obtained by dividing the speed of light by the Hubble constant. With the value derived from Planck, 67.4 km/s per megaparsec, it is about 14.5 billion light-years; with the one measured from Cepheids and supernovae, 73.0, it falls to about 13.4. The difference between the two measurements, known as the Hubble tension, is not yet resolved.

mom-z14.name: MoM-z14
mom-z14.desc: MoM-z14 is a galaxy observed by the James Webb telescope at redshift 14.44, that is, as it was just 280 million years after the Big Bang. At confirmation, published in January 2026, it was the most distant galaxy known. Its light has travelled for about 13.5 billion years, but because of the expansion of the Universe the galaxy is today about 34 billion light-years away.

universo-osservabile.name: Observable universe
universo-osservabile.desc: The observable universe is the sphere, centred on the Earth, from which light has had time to reach us since the beginning of the expansion. Its present radius is about 14,300 megaparsecs, so the diameter is about 93 billion light-years. It is larger than the age of the universe, about 13.8 billion years, would suggest, because in the meantime space has expanded.

universo-intero.name: Entire universe
universo-intero.desc: Nobody knows the size of the entire universe, that is, of everything that exists beyond the part we can observe: it could be finite or infinite. Measurements by the WMAP satellite indicate that the curvature of space is zero to within 0.4%, a result compatible with an infinite universe but not proving it. The size shown here is therefore only a convention, not a measurement.
